cards.explanation: The answer is "How long will the wicked exult." Verse 3 says, "How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?" He says it twice in a row. I think a question that comes out twice has been sitting on him a while. And notice he takes it straight to the LORD.

The answer is people. Verse 5 says, "They crush Your people, O LORD; they oppress Your heritage." The writer is telling the LORD about the people who belong to Him. He says it straight to Him, no sugarcoating.

The answer is True. In verse 7 the wicked say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed." That's their whole theory, and the writer is about to answer it. It's a theory with no homework behind it, friends.

The answers are ear and eye. Verse 9 says, "He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?" In verse 7 the wicked said, "The LORD does not see…" The writer's comeback asks whether the One who formed the eye does not see. The One who put the ear on the head surely hears, and that's pretty hard to argue with.

The answer is False. Verse 10 asks, "He who admonishes the nations, does He not discipline? He who teaches man, does He lack knowledge?" It's a question, not a statement that the LORD lacks knowledge. The writer asks it about the One who teaches man.
The answer is futile. Verse 11 says, "The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile." The LORD knows them all, even the 2 a.m. ones that go nowhere. I've had a few plans like that myself.

The answer is the man the LORD disciplines and teaches. Verse 12 says, "Blessed is the man You discipline, O LORD, and teach from Your law…" I bet discipline isn't the first thing most of us would put on a blessing list. Disciplined and taught, and still called blessed.

The answer is to grant him relief from days of trouble. Verses 12 and 13 read, "Blessed is the man You discipline, O LORD, and teach from Your law, to grant him relief from days of trouble…" The trouble is still named in the verse, and so is the relief. Discipline and teaching on one side, relief on the other, all in one sentence.

The answer is forsake. Verse 14 says, "For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage." The wicked crush them, and the writer still says that. I know a little about sitting in the dark of a junk drawer for years, so that line lands with me.

The answer is righteous. Verse 15 says, "Surely judgment will again be righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it." He says it after listing everything the wicked did. That's some steady faith, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says, "Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence." That's what would have happened without the LORD's help. He says the LORD was his helper.

The answer is supports. In verse 18 the writer says that if he says his foot is slipping, then "Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me." Picture slipping on a floor covered in flour. That loving devotion is what holds him up.

The answer is the LORD's consolation. Verse 19 says, "When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul." The writer doesn't hide the anxiety. He names it, and then he names what delights his soul anyway.

The answer is his stronghold and his rock. Verse 22 says, "But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge." The wicked are ganging up, and the writer says that. A stronghold and a rock don't wobble.

The answer is True. Verse 23 says, "He will bring upon them their own iniquity and destroy them for their wickedness." The writer says it plainly, and he says it with confidence. The verse ends, "The LORD our God will destroy them."
